pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Dinosaurs Were Real (ages 5–7): dinosaurs were REAL animals that lived on Earth an enormously long time ago and are now extinct — none are alive today, and they did not live alongside people.
• Standards — UK (DfE): no direct statutory dinosaur content at KS1, but sits on Y2 science 'Living things and their habitats' (distinguish things that are living, dead, and things that have never been alive) and KS1 History 'events beyond living memory'; forward-anchors to Y3 'Rocks' (fossils) and Y6 'Evolution and inheritance'.
• Standards — US (NGSS): no K–2 dinosaur-specific PE; nearest anchor is grade-3 3-LS4-1 (analyse fossils to provide evidence of organisms that lived long ago) toward which this builds; the 'long ago / extinct' idea is foundational informal-science content here.
• Operational details — Two ideas to secure: (1) REAL, not made up — dinosaurs are known from real bones/fossils, unlike dragons or cartoon monsters; (2) EXTINCT + DEEP TIME — 'extinct' means none are left alive anywhere, and dinosaurs died out long before there were any people (bust the Flintstones 'cavemen + dinosaurs' coexistence myth with a simple time gap). Keep numbers concrete-relative ('a very, very long time ago — long before grandparents, before people at all') rather than millions-of-years abstraction at this age.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (concrete, ~5): says dinosaurs were real animals and that there are none alive now. Tier B (~6): explains 'extinct' as none left alive anywhere, and names dinosaurs as living long ago. Tier C (~7): states dinosaurs lived long before people (not at the same time) and that we know they were real because of fossils.
bestPractices: Lead with 'real animals, known from real bones' and explicitly contrast with made-up creatures (dragons) so 'real vs pretend' is the anchoring distinction.
Teach 'extinct' concretely as 'none left alive anywhere' and connect to the Y2 living/dead/never-lived sorting children already meet.
Directly confront the coexistence myth (people + dinosaurs together): show a simple time gap so children learn dinosaurs were gone long before any people existed.
Use relative time language ('before grandparents, before any people, a very very long time ago') rather than abstract millions — deep-time number sense is not developmentally available yet.
Anchor 'how do we know they were real?' in fossils/bones you can see in a museum, seeding the fossils-as-evidence idea.
keyRepresentations: A simple deep-time ribbon/timeline with 'dinosaurs' far from 'people/now', showing the gap.
A sorting frame: alive today vs only known from fossils (e.g. elephant vs dinosaur), and real vs pretend (dinosaur vs dragon).
Museum fossil skeleton photos as the 'proof they were real'.
A 'long ago' vs 'last year' comparison to build the sense of scale.
commonMisconceptions: 'Dinosaurs and people (cavemen) lived at the same time' — dinosaurs died out long before any humans existed.
'Dinosaurs are made up, like dragons' — dinosaurs were real animals known from real fossils.
'Some dinosaurs are still alive today' (confusing them with living reptiles like crocodiles or lizards) — non-bird dinosaurs are all extinct.
'Extinct means asleep / hiding / will come back' — extinct means none are left alive anywhere.
'All dinosaurs lived at the same time' — different dinosaurs lived in different ages (introduced more fully later).

learn.summary: For children aged 5–7 learning that dinosaurs were real animals that lived an enormously long time ago and that the non-bird dinosaurs (such as T. rex) are now extinct. Two load-bearing ideas: (1) dinosaurs were REAL, known from real bones/fossils, unlike made-up creatures such as dragons; (2) non-bird dinosaurs are EXTINCT (none left alive anywhere) and died out long before any people existed, so people and non-bird dinosaurs never lived together (birds are the one dinosaur group still alive). Use relative time language ('before grandparents, before any people, a very very long time ago') rather than abstract millions of years. The preferred route lets children discover the coexistence myth by placing time markers themselves; alternatives (a museum scene, a few picture questions, a palaeontologist character) are retained for different purposes.

activities.title: Time ribbon: place the markers and find the gap
feedback: When a child places people beside dinosaurs: gently stretch the gap and say 'The big dinosaurs like T. rex were gone long, long before any people were born' — let the correction come from acting, not just being told.
'Grandparents and now' sit close together at one end; 'first people' are a little further; 'dinosaurs' are very far away — point to how big the empty space is between dinosaurs and people.
If a child asks 'how long?', answer in relative terms: 'longer than grandparents, longer than any people — a very, very long time.'
activities.rationale: The coexistence misconception is reinforced by popular media; letting the child try to place people beside dinosaurs and then revealing the gap confronts the myth through the child's own action rather than contradiction. Relative time language fits this age because abstract deep-time number sense is not yet developmentally available.
sourceClaims: Non-avian dinosaurs are extinct and died out long before humans existed; humans and (non-bird) dinosaurs never coexisted — a common misconception reinforced by popular media.
learnerActions: Take a simple long time ribbon/strip and a handful of markers: 'dinosaurs', 'the first people', 'grandparents', 'now'.
Place each marker where you think it belongs along the ribbon.
If you put 'people' next to 'dinosaurs', watch as the grown-up (or the app) stretches the ribbon to open up a huge empty gap, moving 'people' far away from 'dinosaurs'.
Say out loud what the gap shows: the big dinosaurs like T. rex were gone long, long before any people were born.
activities.intendedInsight: Non-bird dinosaurs (like T. rex) lived an enormously long time ago and died out long before any people existed — people and these dinosaurs never lived at the same time (busting the cartoon 'cave people + dinosaurs' myth).

activities.title: Two sorters: alive-today vs only-fossils, and real vs pretend
feedback: Confirm the fossil photo as the 'proof they were real' — real bones, teeth and footprints turned to rock that you could see in a museum.
For the dragon: we have never found any dragon bones or fossils, but we have found real dinosaur bones — that is how we know dinosaurs were real and dragons are made-up.

If a child says a dinosaur like T. rex is still alive somewhere: 'Extinct means none are left alive anywhere — not hiding, not asleep.' Distinguish from rare-but-living animals. (If a child says birds are dinosaurs, that is right: birds are the one dinosaur group still alive.)
Watch for confusing dinosaurs with living reptiles (crocodiles, lizards): non-bird dinosaurs are all extinct.
activities.rationale: 'Real vs pretend' anchored in visible fossil evidence addresses the 'dinosaurs are made up' misconception, and the alive/fossil sort connects extinction to the living/dead/never-alive distinction children meet in KS1 science.
sourceClaims: UK KS1 science requires pupils to distinguish things that are living, dead, and things that have never been alive (Y2 'Living things and their habitats'), the foundation for understanding 'extinct'.
Non-avian dinosaurs are extinct and died out long before humans existed; humans and (non-bird) dinosaurs never coexisted — a common misconception reinforced by popular media.
learnerActions: Sort animals into 'alive today' or 'only known from fossils': crocodile, elephant, chicken, T. rex. (The crocodile, elephant and chicken stay in 'alive today'; T. rex moves to 'only fossils'.)
Sort pictures into 'real' or 'pretend': a dinosaur vs a dragon.
When you tap/choose the dinosaur, look at the photo of its actual museum bones that appears; the dragon gets a 'made-up' tag.
Say why a dinosaur is 'real' and a dragon is 'pretend'.
activities.intendedInsight: Dinosaurs were real animals known from real bones/fossils, unlike made-up creatures; 'extinct' means none are left alive anywhere, as with T. rex and the other non-bird dinosaurs, and this connects to sorting things that are alive, dead, or never alive.

activities.title: Museum-hall scene: bones, time signpost, and 'is it alive today?'
feedback: Confirm the bones as the evidence that dinosaurs were real animals.
Reinforce 'long before people' and 'extinct — none of this kind of dinosaur left alive anywhere' with each reveal.
activities.rationale: A single scene with tappable captions teaches 'real (here are the bones)' and 'long ago' cleanly, but it shows fixed states. It is offered as a scaffold alongside the time-ribbon, which lets the child test the coexistence idea by acting.
sourceClaims: Non-avian dinosaurs are extinct and died out long before humans existed; humans and (non-bird) dinosaurs never coexisted — a common misconception reinforced by popular media.
learnerActions: Explore a scene with a dinosaur skeleton and a present-day street.
Tap/look at the skeleton to reveal 'real bones, real animal'.
Tap/look at a 'time signpost' to reveal 'lived long before people'.
Lift a flap on 'is it alive today?' to reveal 'no — extinct'.
activities.intendedInsight: Dinosaurs were real (here are the bones), lived long ago, and are extinct.

activities.title: Talk it through: diagnostic and deeper probes
feedback: Full answer: dinosaurs were real animals, not made up like dragons — we know because we find their fossils (real bones, teeth and footprints turned to rock); no people lived at the same time as non-bird dinosaurs; they died out a very, very long time before any people, and extinct means none are left alive anywhere.
If a child says dinosaurs are pretend: show fossils are real evidence you can see in a museum; we have never found dragon fossils.
If a child says cave people lived with dinosaurs: stretch the timeline so people are a dot at the very end, far after dinosaurs died out.

If a child says dinosaurs like T. rex are still alive/hiding: clarify 'extinct' means none left alive anywhere; distinguish from rare-but-living animals. If a child means birds, agree that birds are the one dinosaur group still alive today.
Offer a palaeontologist or museum-guide character to answer 'were they real?' and 'are any alive?' in child-friendly language if a conversational format helps engagement.
activities.rationale: The diagnostic surfaces both halves of the concept: a child who thinks dinosaurs are imaginary can't explain the fossil evidence, and a child who pictures cave people with dinosaurs collapses the time gap. The deeper probes force the reasoning out. A friendly character can answer the big questions, though open dialogue is harder to steer for this age and factual target.
sourceClaims: Non-avian dinosaurs are extinct and died out long before humans existed; humans and (non-bird) dinosaurs never coexisted — a common misconception reinforced by popular media.
learnerActions: Respond to a friend's claim: 'Dinosaurs are just pretend, like dragons and unicorns — and anyway, cave people used to keep them as pets.' Is your friend right or wrong?
Explain how we can be so sure dinosaurs were real.
Say whether people ever lived at the same time as dinosaurs.

Answer the deeper questions: How do we know dinosaurs were real if nobody ever saw one alive? Was 'a long time ago' like when grandparents were little, or much, much longer? What does 'extinct' mean, and can you name another extinct animal?
activities.intendedInsight: A full understanding holds all three: dinosaurs were real (evidence = fossils); non-bird dinosaurs like T. rex are extinct (none left alive anywhere); and they lived long before any people.

constraints: Keep time language relative ('before grandparents, before any people, a very, very long time ago') rather than abstract millions of years at this age — deep-time number sense is not yet developmentally available.
The museum scene shows fixed states; it does not let the child test the coexistence idea by acting. Pair it with the time-ribbon where the child places markers and discovers the gap.

Picture multiple-choice questions can check or reinforce the ideas, but recognition alone does not surface the coexistence misconception through the child's own action or build the deep-time feel the way the time-ribbon does; they are well suited to checking.
Open dialogue with a character is engaging but hard to steer for a simple factual target at ages 5–7; keep questions tightly focused.
Distinguish non-bird dinosaurs (all extinct) from living reptiles such as crocodiles and lizards, which children may confuse with still-living dinosaurs.
Anchor 'how do we know?' in fossils/bones that can be seen in a museum, seeding fossils-as-evidence toward later learning (Y3 Rocks, grade-3 fossils).

Checkpoint levels: concrete (~5) — says dinosaurs were real and none alive now; (~6) — explains 'extinct' as none left alive anywhere and that dinosaurs lived long ago; (~7) — states dinosaurs lived long before people and that fossils show they were real.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Both listed sources carry verified:false in the original row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original 'correctAnswer' and some reteach notes state dinosaurs died out 'millions of years ago' while the pedagogy guidance recommends avoiding abstract millions at this age; all learner-facing activities use relative time language, and the factual 'millions of years' is retained only in adult/teacher framing, not shown to the child.

The original artefact comparison claimed a 3D environment 'adds spectacle but no understanding' and that a static picture or quiz cannot build/surface the concept. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established efficacy claims, and have been softened to scoped affordance limits rather than universal laws.
No new evidence of comparative effectiveness between formats is asserted; the preference for the hands-on time-ribbon is a pedagogical proposal.

'Chicken' is used as an 'alive today' example as in the original and is factually correct (a chicken is alive today). Note that birds are living (avian) dinosaurs, a nuance beyond this age band and in tension with the 'non-bird dinosaurs are extinct' framing used elsewhere; it is deliberately not raised in the child-facing sort.

The dragon 'made-up' feedback has been reworded from 'there are no dragon bones anywhere' to 'we have never found any dragon bones or fossils' to anchor the fossils-as-evidence contrast without stating an unqualified absolute to a young child.

probeDeeper: How do we actually know dinosaurs were real if nobody ever saw one alive?
Was 'a long time ago' like when your grandparents were little, or much, much longer than that?
What does it mean when we say an animal is 'extinct'? Can you name another extinct animal?
assess.correctAnswer: Wrong on both counts. Dinosaurs were real animals, not made up like dragons — we know because we find their fossils: real bones, teeth and footprints turned to rock. And no people lived at the same time as (non-bird) dinosaurs; the dinosaurs died out (went extinct) millions of years ago, long before there were any people. Extinct means none are left alive anywhere.

errorPatterns.pattern: Dinosaurs are make-believe, like dragons and monsters.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that fossils are real evidence — bones and footprints in rock you can touch in a museum; contrast with dragons, which leave none.
errorPatterns.distractor: My friend is right — dinosaurs are just pretend, like dragons.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says dinosaurs are pretend or not real.

errorPatterns.pattern: People (cave people) lived at the same time as dinosaurs — the cartoon overlap.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Stretch out the timeline: dinosaurs died out millions of years before the first people; use a long timeline where humans are a dot at the very end.
errorPatterns.distractor: Cave people did keep dinosaurs — they lived together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says humans and dinosaurs shared the Earth.

errorPatterns.pattern: Some dinosaurs are still alive somewhere, hiding in a jungle or on an island.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Clarify 'extinct' — none left alive anywhere; distinguish from rare-but-living animals.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says not all died out, or that some might still be found.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks dinosaurs are imaginary, or that people/cave people lived alongside them.
responseLevels.full: States dinosaurs were real (evidence = fossils), are extinct (none left), and lived long before any people — keeping the huge time gap and transferring 'extinct' to another animal.
responseLevels.partial: Knows dinosaurs were real but is fuzzy on extinction or the time gap — thinks some might still be alive, or that it was only a little while ago.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Your friend says 'Dinosaurs are just pretend, like dragons and unicorns — and anyway, cave people used to keep them as pets.' Is your friend right or wrong? Explain how we can be so sure dinosaurs were real, and whether people ever lived at the same time as them.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks dinosaurs are imaginary can't explain the fossil evidence; a child who pictures cave people with dinosaurs collapses the huge time gap. Only a child holding 'real + extinct + long before people' answers both halves, and the tier-two 'how do we know / did people live with them' forces that reasoning out.
